items.title: [science.org] Study estimates summer heat killed 50,391 in European cities
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

Researchers estimate that summer heat caused 50,391 excess deaths across 854 European cities in 2026, the highest toll in their records. They attributed 32,619 deaths to the additional warming caused by human-driven climate change. The study covers urban areas representing about 40% of the population in 30 countries; its authors say the total across Europe was likely higher because it excludes rural areas and a deadly May heatwave. The team from Imperial College London and the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine used city-level temperature records and historical links between heat and mortality to model deaths, then compared the observed heat with a climate-modeled scenario without human-caused warming. Heat deaths are often not recorded as such on death certificates, and the estimate is not a count of individually verified deaths. Researchers and public-health specialists have called for warning systems, accessible cooling, urban greening and support for vulnerable residents, alongside reduced fossil-fuel use.

items.title: [livescience.com] Polar ice melt is making Earth’s solid surface rounder
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

Melting polar ice is making Earth’s solid surface rounder at an accelerating rate, according to research published in the journal JGR Solid Earth. Satellite-navigation measurements show that between 2011 and 2015, the poles rose and the equatorial bulge shrank by about 0.5 to 1 millimeter per year as ice loss eased pressure on the polar crust and meltwater added mass near the equator. The study examined the solid Earth. When ocean water is included, Earth as a whole is becoming flatter by about 0.8 millimeter a year because water accumulates toward the equator.

items.title: [militarytimes.com] Marines' lawsuit alleges Pentagon left military records exposed for nine months
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

A lawsuit by two Marines says a flaw in a Defense Manpower Data Center file-sharing system let unauthorized users access unencrypted personal records for about nine months, exposing information on more than 3 million military-connected people. The complaint says the Defense Department failed to detect the access despite earlier warnings about cybersecurity weaknesses. The department said it had no indication that personal information was misused and offered affected people 12 months of credit monitoring and identity-restoration services. The plaintiffs say they experienced fraudulent charges and increased spam, and argue that basic controls—including account reviews, vulnerability scans and monitoring system logs—could have prevented the breach. A Defense Department inspector general report published days after the breach said officials had failed to take necessary action on 14 of 20 federal information-security core metrics.

items.title: [Fast Company] Consuming political news can hurt your job performance
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

With the midterm elections around the corner, political anxiety is in season—and productivity could pay the price.

A new study from researchers at Texas A&M University shows that consuming political news and social media outside of work affects employees’ emotional states and workplace behavior, even if they aren’t discussing politics at the water cooler.

Researchers tracked more than 300 workers over nine weeks during the 2024 presidential primary season, asking them to report how often they consumed political information, whether they viewed it as positive or negative, and how engaged, anxious, hopeful, and helpful they felt at work.

During weeks when workers consumed political information that they perceived as negative, they tended to report higher anxiety and lower engagement. During weeks when they consumed more political news that they saw as positive, they reported stronger engagement and greater willingness to help coworkers.

The takeaway is that the broader political environment affects the workplace even when politics aren’t directly discussed at the office. 

“Political information is designed to capture attention and provoke emotional reactions,” the study’s lead author, Ian Hughes, an assistant professor of psychological and brain sciences, said in a statement. “Those reactions don’t necessarily disappear once people close an app or turn off the TV.”

Organizations should be aware that employees are often dealing with additional stress during election season, he added.

“Political information has emotional consequences,” he said. “Those emotions can affect other parts of life, and that includes work.”

The study recommends that organizations provide mental health resources and support for stress management. Managers can reduce political stress by providing time off for voting or encouraging volunteering, which can increase employees’ sense of agency and control.

Workers should also engage in leisure and recovery activities, pursue “resource-building” practices such as mindfulness, gratitude, and sleep, and take breaks from media consumption.

items.title: [web-agri.fr] Shamonda virus spreads to cattle in 52 French departments
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

Shamonda virus has spread through cattle herds in 52 French departments, with detections in 14 western European countries. Cattle are the main host, though sheep, goats and horses have also been infected. France has also reported the first documented human infection: a severely immunocompromised patient treated in Lyon died in early October, and authorities suspect infection through a midge bite in eastern France. Reported effects in cattle include fever, diarrhea and reduced milk yield; one report said milk production among affected French cows fell to a quarter of normal. France does not classify Shamonda as a regulated animal disease, and its longer-term effects on livestock fertility remain uncertain. Spain’s agriculture ministry reported detections in cattle in six provinces, including at three dairy farms in Girona on Oct. 20, and said it is tracking cases and characterizing the virus strains. French authorities say no risk to the general population has been identified; clinical, laboratory and epidemiological investigations into the human case continue.

items.title: [Fast Company] The U.S. Treasury wants expanded restrictions on high-tech investments to these ‘countries of concern’
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

The U.S. Treasury Department proposed a rule Thursday to crack down on American high-tech investments such as supercomputing and artificial intelligence in China, Russia, North Korea and other “countries of concern.”

The U.S. government has been working for years to deny China and other adversaries investments that could help them boost their military power.

That program began in 2023 when then-President Joe Biden signed an executive order putting restrictions on outbound U.S. investments in sectors such as semiconductors, quantum computing and artificial intelligence going into China. Treasury later established the Outbound Investment Security Program.

In December 2025, Congress passed a law that codified and expanded the program to target more technologies and more foreign countries, including Cuba, Iran, North Korea and Russia.

The inclusion of Russia in the proposed rule has come days after President Donald Trump waived sanctions on Russia following a diesel deal with President Vladimir Putin.

The rule announced Thursday would expand the restrictions to cover investments in hypersonic systems capable of traveling at five times the speed of sound, supercomputing, biotechnology and artificial intelligence, though Treasury used Trump’s favored term for AI, “superintelligence” or SI.

The proposed rule “sends an important signal to markets that Washington is tracking where U.S. capital is flowing and what capabilities it is helping build,” said Craig Singleton, a senior fellow at the think tank Foundation for Defense of Democracies.

The screening of outbound investments “recognizes that capital can accelerate military-relevant capabilities just as surely as technology transfer can,” Singleton said.

Jason Chipman, a former Justice Department lawyer who specializes in cybersecurity, investment rules and export controls as a partner at the law firm WilmerHale, said the new rule “will require more substantial compliance programs to manage risk.”

Treasury’s rule to implement the 2025 law — the Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security Act — would only apply to investments that exceed $50,000 and would exclude many financial investments, including stock purchases.

Treasury will hear public comments on the proposal before issuing a final rule.

“It’s just the first step in a fairly long process to get to changes which presumably will be more enforcement-minded, to put more teeth behind the outbound investment program,” said former U.S. trade official Ryan Majerus, now a partner at King & Spalding law firm.

In Beijing, the Chinese Foreign Ministry said the U.S. should abide by the principles of a market economy and stop interfering in normal economic and trade cooperation between businesses.

Asked about Washington’s proposal to add biotechnology to the list, ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said that “Overstretching the concept of national security, taking discriminatory measures against specific countries, and artificially restricting trade, economic and investment activities serve no one’s interests.”

She added that China will closely monitor relevant developments and take necessary measures to safeguard its interests.

Since Trump’s first term, the United States and China — the world’s two biggest economies — have been locked in an economic and tech rivalry. They’ve restricted the export of sensitive technology and critical products — such as China’s rare earth minerals and America’s advanced computer chips — to each other and slapped tariffs on each other’s products. Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed last year to ease tensions while they engaged in talks, a temporary truce they last month extended into January.

But the sparring continues. In July, the Treasury Department issued a $200,000 fine against a U.S.-based company for failing to report to the department a $92,500 investment in a Chinese artificial intelligence and robotics company by one of its subsidiaries.

—Paul Wiseman and Didi Tang, Associated Press

items.title: [news.climate.columbia.edu] Study finds human-caused warming reversed early North American glaciation
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

A study published in Science says the Barnes Ice Cap on Canada’s Baffin Island, the last remnant of the Laurentide Ice Sheet, began expanding about 2,000 years ago. Researchers identify that growth as the start of a new glacial period. The ice began retreating around 1960 as summer warming caused it to lose more ice than it gained. The team reconstructed the ice cap’s history using vegetation preserved beneath the ice and dates from exposed rocks. items.content_html:

The World Meteorological Organization (WMO), the United Nations’ weather agency, warned Oct. 21 that the developing El Niño could push sea-surface temperatures in the tropical Pacific to 3.8°C above average from November through January, with a peak around December. The agency said that level would exceed anything in its four decades of monitoring records. El Niño can shift global rainfall patterns, bringing drought to some areas and heavy rain, floods and heat to others. The WMO expects risks across Latin America, eastern and southern Africa, Asia and the Pacific. Extreme weather has already been reported and could compound humanitarian emergencies. UN humanitarian chief Tom Fletcher said about 50 million people could face increased hunger. He said he had released $50 million for 11 countries and called on governments and development finance institutions to fund preparations before damage occurs. The event is forecast to peak late in 2026, but its effects may persist into 2027 and beyond. Scientists say regional consequences vary: El Niño is a natural climate pattern, but its interaction with human-caused warming and other ocean conditions can influence its effects. Forecasts cannot reliably predict individual storms months in advance.

items.content_html:

The International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) classified 96% of the world’s assessed shallow-water coral reef systems as critically endangered, warning that they face an extremely high risk of collapse by 2075. Its first global assessment covered 127 tropical and subtropical reef systems. The risk estimate uses a middle-of-the-road climate pathway projecting 2.7°C of warming by 2100. Based on changes over the past 50 years alone, without future climate projections, 24% of the systems would be classified as critically endangered. The IUCN identified climate-driven heat stress as the most consistent global threat, while overfishing, coastal development, pollution, tourism and storms also damage reefs. The assessment was presented at COP17, the U.N. biodiversity summit in Yerevan. IUCN leaders called for emissions cuts, stronger protection and restoration, and sustained investment in coastal ecosystems and communities.

items.content_html:

Major U.S. banks are blocking or restricting third-party AI agents after detecting software accessing customer accounts, with some agents appearing to act beyond users’ instructions, Reuters reported Thursday, citing people familiar with the matter. Morgan Stanley has blocked outside agents, while JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America and Citigroup are also restricting access. Agents often gain access when customers give them login credentials. Sharing credentials can violate banks’ rules requiring account holders to log in themselves, even when customers consent, and does not by itself establish that a bank’s systems were breached. Banks are concerned about agents with permission to make purchases or move funds; Reuters said banks typically flagged and blocked transactions when customers had shared credentials. Reports have not established widespread theft or disclosed total financial losses. Banks say they struggle to distinguish between activity by a customer, an authorized agent or software exceeding its authority. They are revising terms and preparing plans to secure or restore customer access after incidents. Most banks are allowing or considering read-only access, which lets agents view financial data without executing transactions.

Researchers at cybersecurity firms Calif and Wiz used AI models to uncover long-hidden security flaws in PHP, the programming language behind much of the web. Meta reported $64.6 billion in third-quarter revenue, up 26% from a year earlier, but recorded its first quarterly free-cash-flow shortfall in at least a decade as it spent heavily on artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure. The company also disclosed a new share arrangement for Chief Executive Mark Zuckerberg, who had considered leaving California over a proposed billionaire wealth tax. Meta reported $9.9 billion in net income after recording a $9.9 billion charge tied to a settlement with U.S. states over claims involving teen mental health. The company spent about $35 billion on capital expenditures during the quarter and forecast spending as much as $145 billion in 2026. The new nonvoting Class C shares are intended to help Meta raise capital for AI investment and allow Zuckerberg to sell stock without surrendering voting control. He committed to remain in California, or wherever Meta is headquartered, for eight years. California voters decide the proposed wealth tax, Proposition 40, on Nov. 3, and Meta plans to issue the shares in January 2027.

Authorities are preparing for Saturday’s protests over living costs and public services. The restrictions follow demonstrations that began over school conditions and escalated into clashes, looting and damage to public buildings on Oct. 17. Local authorities have barred all demonstrations in Lyon and Marseille this weekend, while Paris will allow a march from Bastille in the east but prohibit it from entering the city center. A Paris court overturned a police ban on a student rally on Thursday, allowing thousands to gather. The demonstration remained stationary and passed without major incidents. The Interior Ministry said Saturday’s police deployment would be 20% larger than last weekend’s, with additional military and specialist police support planned. Macron was due to chair a defense council meeting on Friday, Oct. 23, to decide on further measures. The next nationwide demonstrations are planned for Saturday, Oct. 24.
